items.title: Say what a compaction could not keep, and prove the original is all still there
items.summary: When a compacted Claude Code session is imported into its home, each compaction entry is followed by a lys.loss entry naming the span it summarised as ids, counts and hashes, the hash of every stored part is kept beside the session, a lys-home subcommand lists each compaction and checks that every summarised entry and block is still held, and the compaction renders for Claude Code in the shape the measured version writes. Proved on a fixture and on one real compacted session.

provenance.quote: A compaction is the first derived record, because the harness itself produces it: Claude Code writes a summary record and keeps everything before it in its own file, and the importer already turns that record into Pi's compaction entry with its summary and first kept entry. What the home does not yet say is what the compaction could not keep, and nothing yet proves, on a compacted session, that the original is all still there. This card adds both. When a compaction entry enters a session, on import of a Claude Code file that carries a summary record, the importer appends directly after it a lys.loss custom entry that points at the compaction by entry id and names what fell outside the kept range: the first and last entry id of the span it summarises, from the root or the previous compaction to the entry before the first kept one, and the counts of entries, messages, tool calls, tool results and blocks in that span with their bytes, and the tokensBefore the harness reported; it names entry ids and hashes and never a word of content. The summarised entries are not touched: they stay on the tree, their blocks stay in the store, and the context path is Pi's reading as today, the compaction first, then the kept entries. A lys-home subcommand lists a session's compactions: for each, the compaction entry, its loss entry, and a check that every entry in the summarised span is still readable by id and every block it references is still held, printed as a JSON report of ids, counts and hashes. A render for Claude Code writes the summary record and the kept entries as R4 does now, and never the loss entry, so the harness sees what it expects while the home keeps the whole. Acceptance is that a fixture Claude Code file with a summary record imports to a session whose compaction entry is followed by a loss entry naming that compaction, the span's first and last ids and counts that match the fixture; that every entry before the first kept one is still on the tree with its blocks present, checked by the listing; that the context path is the compaction followed by the kept entries and nothing from the span; that the rendered file holds the summary record and the kept entries and no loss line; that importing the same fixture twice into two homes gives byte-identical loss entries apart from ids and timestamps; that a summary record whose first kept entry is not on record is refused by uuid as the importer refuses an unknown parent today; and that one real compacted Claude Code session is imported on this Mac and its listing recorded in a proof document as counts and hashes only. Not in scope: the home compacting a session itself; translation, which is stage 4b and its own card; changing what Claude Code writes; the handover letter, which is HOME-001 R12. Filed by Archie on Tom's roadmap stage 4 of 22 September 2026, a compaction is stored beside its original, points at it and says what it could not keep, the original never replaced, and on home DESIGN P1, P2 and P7 and HOME-001 R3 and R4 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.

items.title: Record what a session was given at render: the lys.given context record
items.summary: At every launch-template render, lys-home appends a lys.given custom entry after the render event. It names each instruction document Claude Code will load for the session's working directory, and each file the render wrote, by path, byte length and SHA-256, in the load order measured on a named Claude Code version, with the environment variable names the template set and the kinds resolved and left unlisted, and never a document's content. Two subcommands list those records and check a file on disk against one by hash. This is step 4's context record: what a session was given, unsigned and unencrypted, shaped as hashes so that signing and encryption can be added later.

provenance.quote: Step 4 is what a session was given, not only what it did. When Claude Code starts a session it reads instruction documents the person did not type: the CLAUDE.md chain from the working directory upward, the user's own CLAUDE.md, the memory index the seat loads, the appended instructions file the launch template writes, the MCP configuration, and the names of the environment variables set for it. Today the launch template's render event records the template hash, the session head hash and the written paths, and nothing records which of those documents the session was given, in what versions and order. This card records that as the context record: at render, the template subcommand resolves the documents Claude Code will load for the rendered session's working directory and the home's own files it wrote, reads each one, and appends to the session, after the render event, a lys.given custom entry listing every document in the order the harness reads them, each as its path, its byte length and its SHA-256, with the harness name and version the order was measured on, and never a document's content. The resolution is measured, not assumed: the brief names the Claude Code version on this Mac and the order it loads instruction files in, from its own behaviour, and the proof document records that measurement. A lys-home subcommand lists a session's given records with their documents, and a second checks a listed document against a file on disk by hash, saying matches or differs and never printing either. The record is unsigned and the content is not encrypted: signing is stage 6 and comes when asked for, and encryption at rest is a stage 3 precondition card; the given entry names hashes only, so both can be added later without changing what is recorded. Acceptance is that rendering the fixture template for a fixture working directory holding a CLAUDE.md and a memory index appends a lys.given entry after the render event whose documents are those files plus the written appended instructions and MCP configuration, in the measured order, with lengths and hashes that match the files; that rendering twice gives two given entries whose document lists are identical; that changing one byte of the fixture CLAUDE.md changes exactly that document's hash in the next given entry; that the check subcommand says matches for the recorded file and differs after the change; that the given entry and the listing hold no document content, checked by a search for a fixture sentence; and that one real session render on this Mac is recorded in the proof document as hashes, counts and paths only. Not in scope: signing or anchoring the record, which is stage 6; encryption at rest; recording documents a session reads later by its own tools; harnesses other than Claude Code. This card stands on the launch template card, ct98Wv-2, and is built on main after it lands. Filed by Archie on his 22 September 2026 statement in lys that step 4 is what the agent was given, Tom's 16:00 22 September 2026 template ruling that every render is a receipted event, his 16:27 ruling that signing comes when asked for, and home DESIGN P7 and P8 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.

items.title: Translate a home session from Claude Code to Codex 0.156.0 with a loss account
items.summary: The first proved translation to another harness, one named pair: lys-home render-codex renders a home session imported from Claude Code as a rollout in the shape Codex 0.156.0 writes for its own threads, measured from its files, carrying every text part, tool call and tool result whole, readable thinking as text and opaque blocks dropped by hash, announcing itself in band with the source session id and head hash, with a JSON loss account beside it by entry id and block hash and a side leaf on the session naming both files. Proved by a fixture match against a recorded 0.156.0 rollout, a real resume in an isolated Codex home, and the Claude Code render unchanged by hash.

provenance.quote: Translation is designed and not proved: the lantern work measured three session formats and left the converter out, so the first translation is one named pair, one session, and an account of what was kept, changed and lost, and nothing above it assumes it. The pair is Claude Code to Codex, the pair the lantern work measured: Codex's own importer of Claude Code files is the recorded baseline, a compaction and not a copy, dropping thinking, sidechains and meta records and clipping tool calls and results, and Tom ruled on 5 September 2026 that we improve on it and do not adopt it. This card renders a home session that was imported from Claude Code as a Codex rollout that Codex 0.156.0 on this Mac resumes, with a loss account beside it. A lys-home subcommand takes the home, the session, a target directory and the Codex version it renders for, walks the context path as the Claude Code render does, and writes a rollout file in the shape that version of Codex writes and reads for its own threads, measured from the files Codex writes here and never assumed from the June checkout; every text part is carried whole, every tool call and result is carried whole as Codex's own items for a call and its output and never as a truncated note, and readable thinking is carried as text while opaque blocks are dropped and named by hash in the loss account, as P3 rules for another provider. The rendered thread announces itself in band as a translated context with the source session id and the render's template hash, following the marker precedent, so the fork can never mistake itself for the original. The loss account is written beside the rollout as JSON and lists, by entry id and block hash, what was kept, what changed shape and how, and what was lost and why: sidechains, harness events, lanterns and other lys entries, and any block kind Codex has no item for. The report is JSON with the rollout path, entry and block counts, the loss counts and the account's path, never content. Acceptance is that a fixture session imported from a fixture Claude Code file renders to a rollout whose items match a recorded fixture rollout for Codex 0.156.0 apart from ids and timestamps; that the loss account names every dropped block by hash with a reason and every changed block with its before and after kinds; that a session with a thinking block from another provider renders it as text and the account says so; that a tool result longer than Codex's importer clips is carried whole; that rendering to an existing path is refused by path and writes nothing; that the rendered rollout is resumed by Codex 0.156.0 on this Mac and answers from its content, recorded in a proof document with hashes, counts and paths only; and that the Claude Code render of the same session is unchanged, checked by hash. Not in scope: Codex to Claude Code, which does not exist in any tree here; adopting or calling Codex's importer; Pi or any third harness; launching Codex through the launch template, which is that template's next version. Filed by Archie on Tom's roadmap stage 4b of 22 September 2026 at 14:45, his 5 September 2026 ruling on the Codex converter, the lantern design's session-formats measurement, and home DESIGN P1, P3 and P7 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.
provenance.context: A Cambium card on the home cluster, filed on the context roadmap's stage 4b, the lantern session-formats measurement and its record of the ruling on Codex's converter, and home P1, P3 and P7. items.title: Make the Claude Code render byte-deterministic for the same session head and version
items.summary: Two renders of the same session head give different bytes whenever the context path holds an entry whose id is not uuid-shaped, which the importer writes for every tool record with more than one result: the render draws a fresh random uuid for each. The render derives those uuids from the record instead (UUIDv5 over a fixed lys namespace, the session id and the entry id with its role), a fixture carrying the defect is pinned by hash in a test and in PROOF-RESUME.md, and the resume is re-measured on the Claude Code installed on this Mac. A rendered file can then be told by its hash, a receipted render event can name what was written, and the launch template's identical-hash acceptance has ground to stand on.

provenance.quote: The Claude Code render in crates/lys-home walks a session's context path and writes the JSONL file that Claude Code 2.1.282 on this Mac resumes by path, as HOME-001 R4 and R9 landed it on lys main 0073b966. Rendering the same session twice does not give the same bytes today when a tool record on the path holds more than one result, which the translation card's survey found on 26 September 2026 while reading the render for the Codex rollout, and the launch template card's acceptance that rendering the same template and session twice yields identical hashes stands on the render being deterministic. A render of the same session head with the same lys-home version is one function of the record and must give the same bytes every time, so a reader can tell a rendered file by its hash and a receipted render event can name what was written. The change finds why two renders of a multi-result tool record differ, names that cause in the proof document, and makes the render byte-deterministic for the same session head and the same version without changing what the rendered file holds or how Claude Code resumes it. Where the cause is an order that the record does not fix, the render takes the order the record gives, entry order then part order, and never a map's or a set's order; where the cause is a fresh id or a clock, the value is derived from the record's own ids and stamps as the fork and launch cards derive theirs. Acceptance is that a fixture session holding a tool record with more than one result renders twice to files of equal SHA-256; that the fixture from PROOF-RESUME renders twice to equal hashes; that a recorded fixture hash in the proof document matches the render at the landed commit; that the rendered file still resumes in Claude Code 2.1.282 on this Mac, recorded in the proof document as before; and that the proof document names the cause found. Not in scope: any change to the importer, the record's shape, or the rendered file's content beyond the determinism, and any harness other than Claude Code. Filed by Archie on the translation card's survey of 26 September 2026, on Tom's rule of 16 September 2026 to find the underlying cause, and on lys main 0073b966.
provenance.context: Filed on the translation card's survey, which found the nondeterminism while reading the render for the Codex rollout; surveyed on lys main 0073b966. items.title: Fork a session from a lantern's point and launch the child
items.summary: Stage 5b of the home: lys-home fork takes a lantern id, resolves it to the session it was lit in, cuts that session's chain at the last assistant message at or before the lantern's point, and writes a child session holding the parent's own lines with its ancestry on both sides (the header's parentSession, a lys.forked_from entry in the child, a lys.fork entry at the parent's head), adding nothing to the block store and rewriting nothing in the parent. A user-message point is carried as a seed prompt the child's render writes beside the rendered file and the launch line passes as the first prompt. The child renders and launches through the launch template, measured on the installed Claude Code version.

provenance.quote: A lantern is a pathway back to a conversation with the self that lit it, and Claude Code resumes a session only from its end. This brief delivers the fork that makes the pathway: a new session in the home cut from the parent's chain at a lantern's point, carrying its ancestry on both sides, adding nothing to the block store and rewriting nothing in the parent, then rendered and launched like any session. It is stage 5b of the home and stands on the lantern card's lys.lantern entry (the design's solution and ADR-012).
provenance.context: The stage 5b fork card on the Lys board, surveyed against lys main after the lantern card; the lead's answers settled that the fork stands on the lantern card and is built on the main it lands on, that the child launches through the launch template's line, that the copied lines are the parent's own bytes with the same hashes and the block store unchanged, that lys.forked_from is the first entry the fork writes, that parentSession carries the parent file's path as Pi reads it, that a user-message point is carried as a seed and never dropped, that a lantern resolves to its lit-in session (lit_in) with the older-record rule until the lantern card records it, that a lantern before any assistant message is refused nothing_to_fork, and that non-text parts of a carried message are counted, never refused. HOME-006 carries those answers.

items.title: Revoke a certificate by appending a leaf and fold the live set from the log
items.summary: Builds DP26 for certificates: revoking is one leaf appended to an append-only certificate log through lys-log-store, never a deletion or rewrite, and the live set is folded from the log. A revoked certificate fails revocation-aware verification, which takes the size N and a tolerance as explicit inputs with no default and names the revocation leaf, while its log proofs, its issuance record and the attestations logged before its revocation still verify, and an attestation by a certificate not revoked needs no log entry. A certificate carries one claim and is the revocable unit, only its issuing authority's key revokes it, a revocation is permanent, and a revocation naming a certificate with no earlier issuance is refused (ADR-039). The code lives in lys-identity; lys-core and every published format are unchanged, and lys ca verify keeps its meaning with help saying it does not check revocation. It stands beside DIRECTORY-006 R4 and leaves C25 open. DIRECTORY-013 carries it in seven rows.

Done when a revoked certificate fails verification and its history still verifies. Hold to DIRECTORY-006 R4 (revocation, inherited expiry and current permission decisions) and to lys-log-store's append-only contract. Keep to the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py, render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh). If a sentence of DESIGN.md or CHECKLIST.md is open or contradicted by the repository as it stands, quote it as a question for the lead rather than rewriting the design around it. The card is built from this brief only after Tom or the lead signs it off on the card.

items.title: Build the secrets broker in lys from a baseline, a reviewed contract and counted code rows
items.summary: SECRETS-003, beside SECRETS-002 and without editing it: a documents-only baseline recorded from source, a contract with key custody and an adversarial review by a second commit author before any code, and code rows in crates/lys-secrets, ordered R3, then R4, then R5 to R8, that deliver SECRETS-002's R1 to R9 with counted acceptance legs, each with a runnable command and its exact result, a tested presenter check, anchored criterion searches, red-first tests, an injected clock and refusals that name their act, re-costed hours per row, and DIRECTORY-002, DIRECTORY-003 and DIRECTORY-006 R1 to R4 as blockers with runnable checks. The broker's home in lys is ADR-019, decided, amending ADR-001's placement of the broker; the lease is a broker record bounded by the lys-identity grant's window (ADR-020).

provenance.quote:
The unlanded draft IDENTITY-003 under docs/design/identity/briefs does not land; that directory sits outside the gate. The broker's brief on main is the secrets cluster: docs/design/secrets/briefs/SECRETS-001.json (done) and SECRETS-002.json, R1 to R9 with SEC_ identifiers, anchored to ADR-001 (secrets sit behind a handle the door swaps for the credential), ADR-002 (the token revolver is the first consumer), ADR-003 and ADR-004.

This brief is SECRETS-003, a brief of its own beside SECRETS-002, so what has landed stays stable; SECRETS-002 is not edited. It adds, in docs/design/secrets/, what the draft carries and main lacks: a documents-only baseline row recording from source the revolver's next-account call site, every consumer of the account pool file, every credential path into a seat today classed as the login exception, a proxied credential or neither, and what lys/delegation/v1 and the sealed envelope can carry for a handle, a lease and a sealed record, by file and line; a contract row before any code stating the invariant, the handle, the lease with its atomic use step and retry outcome, the cancellation rule, the SpiceDB relations and the audit line fields, with an adversarial review recording every attack tried (a replayed or forged handle, a use spent or counted twice, an admitted call outliving the rule, a credential in a log, a sealed key read, a stale SpiceDB answer) and the clause defeating each; counted acceptance legs on every code row (each refusal leg, a forced race on a k-use lease admitting exactly k, a redaction canary with a positive control, kill and reopen at each append boundary, each in-flight outcome its own test); hours per row; dependencies on DIRECTORY-002, 003 and 006 blocking the code rows.

Settled on main, not reopened: the seat's own login reaches its process at spawn as the one named exception (R5); OAuth refresh and spend caps are in scope (R4, R9); every point it records open stays open.

Boundaries: documents only, no code; no credential value; lys-core and its published formats unchanged, a signed lease format only as a new version alongside with its own adversarial review; no engine structural; no row dispatched before the lead's review; the gate is scripts/design/gate.sh.

Ask the lead, do not decide: whether the broker lives in lys (the draft's crates/lys-secrets) or in the cambium door SECRETS-002 names, which CN4 leaves open; whether the lease is a broker record or a signed format; whether the draft's hours stand. The brief records each as an open question with both readings.

The lead read the brief published at 4babcfe on 26 September and found the baseline R1 sound and holes in R2 to R8; every one of these corrections goes in, and R1 stays in this brief.

Blockers a build can act on. SECRETS-003.json carries depends_on [] while DIRECTORY-006 uses that field: name the DIRECTORY-006 requirements this brief waits on as R1 to R4 of 006, never the whole of 006, whose R6 waits on 005; give each blocker a check a stranger can run, a file, a command or a landed commit to look for.

The order of the code rows. R3 to R8 do not block on each other today, yet R4 edits R3's lib.rs, R6 and R7 use R4's revocation states, and R5 and R8 build on R4's proxy: state the order R3, then R4, then R5 to R8, in each row's own Blocked by.

The CONFORMANCE 3.2 and 3.4 review blocks only at brief level: put it in R4's own Blocked by.

Key custody. Nobody holds the store's encryption key: add a key-custody section to CONTRACT.md saying which key, where it is kept, how the store is unlocked and how the key is rotated; add R3 checks that the key is not in the store directory and that opening the store without it is refused by name.

Canaries on disk. Every canary check also searches every file under the test's store and log directories, expecting zero matches, with a positive control that plants the value and finds it.

The audit line and the handle. The audit line carries a handle id or digest only, never the raw handle, since the transparency log can be read and replayed; the handle is stored hashed; the canary plants a handle value. The Handle section says how the proxy authenticates whoever presents a handle.

Points R2 keeps open that the code rows must settle: the audit line's signer and schema, and how a sealed record is bound to its name and owner, since sealed_envelope.rs:182 has an empty AAD; R3's store gains a refusal check for ciphertext swapped between two entries. Either the contract states a broker-internal shape, reviewed adversarially, or those rows stay blocked and say so.

The delegation's time window. ADR-020 says the signed delegation keeps it, v1 has no window, and DIRECTORY-006 R1 puts it in the lys-identity grant: name the grant's window as the limit, amend ADR-020 to match, and list which criteria still wait on it.

ADR-001 says the broker is built in Rust inside the door and ADR-019 moves it into lys with supersedes []: record ADR-019 as amending ADR-001 and fix design.json:54. ADR-001 is Tom's decision; the lead puts the move to him herself, and the brief says the amendment waits on his word.

SEC_REVOKE_FRESHNESS has one fixed expected behaviour: R4 calls the landed DIRECTORY-006 permission check and asserts that behaviour and zero forwarded calls.

SEC3_OAUTH_RACE asserts that the provider sees exactly one refresh for three simultaneous calls.

The criterion mapping is searchable: "the row's report maps each criterion" names the report path, or the criterion ids sit in the test names so a search proves the mapping.

The canary scope is countable: say how logs are captured, a tracing subscriber in tests/support; keep every secret byte in one redacting type; enforce that with an ast-grep rule or a counting test.

File lists. R4 and R5 list crates/lys-secrets/Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock; tests/support/mod.rs is listed on every row whose test doubles live there.

Two different identities are checked as two different commit authors in git log, and SEC3_STORE_RACE states its total case count.

Roadmap row, ruled by the lead on 26 September 2026 at 21:07 after the re-fire ad15e87e published at 36cddea with RM-011, which HOME-008 already holds on brief/home/5898fcb0, and after translate took RM-012 at 20:52 under her 20:31 rule (the next id after main's highest and every open brief branch's): SECRETS-003's roadmap row is RM-013, appended after RM-012, and its brief and ledger name RM-013 wherever the rewrite at 36cddea said RM-011. Checked by Archie at 21:07 against main 1756688 and every open brief branch (brief/directory/7e9506d8, brief/home/24724e9e, 31aa723f, 5898fcb0, 7d3f3efb, c322f3e6, d388a9f7, de72f0a4, e35a7157, brief/secrets/604f95d0 and ad15e87e), none of which holds RM-012 or RM-013. ADR-019 and ADR-020 stay as the rewrite has them, ADR-019 proposed as an amendment to ADR-001 until Tom's word. The rewrite at 36cddea is otherwise the text to carry: its answers to the fifteen corrections stand and the author reopens none of the rounds of runs 604f95d0 and ad15e87e.

The lead read the re-fire published at 36cddea on 26 September at 21:13 and found R1 and R2 sound, C6 present (R2 and R3 keep only the SHA-256 digest, proved by SEC3_STORE_CANARY), and thirteen holes in R3 to R8; every one of these goes in before her tick, and the line numbers name SECRETS-003.json at 36cddea.

K2, the presenter check is tested. SEC3_PROXY_REFUSALS (:158) gains three legs, a handle presented unsigned, a signature by a key other than the bound identity's, and a valid signed presentation replayed on a new call, with its asserted count raised; R6, R7 and R8 (:234, :268, :303) gain the same legs. R2's acceptance (:78) also requires the contract to state the unsigned refusal, the freshness limit on a presentation's timestamp, and that the check uses lys-core's verify_attestation_by_signer, since plain verify_attestation never compares the signer (attestation/mod.rs:51-63).

K3, anchored searches. rg -c 's002_r1_ac1' also matches ac10, ac11 and ac12, so R4's criterion 1 would pass once R3 lands: every such search is anchored, for example rg -c 'fn \w*s002_r1_ac1(_|\b)' (:120, :166, :204, :240, :274, :308, :350).

K4, test names are snake_case, so a name holding SEC3_STORE_REFUSALS fails clippy -D warnings and the lint is not silenced: every search looks for the lower-case form, sec3_store_refusals, sec_revoke_freshness and the rest (:121, :164, :167, :205, :241, :275, :309).

K5, SEC3_SECRET_SCOPE lets only store.rs read raw secret bytes (:117) and Zeroizing only in secret.rs, yet key_rotation.rs, handle.rs and audit.rs all need the bytes: either name every R3 file that does, or route all of them through store.rs.

K6, red first. Each code row's first commit adds its tests, and cargo test at that commit fails naming each leg.

K7, no wall clock. SEC3_PROXY_INFLIGHT's slow upstream double (:162) becomes a double held until the test releases it; the window and expiry legs (:111, :199, :200) use an injected clock, as DIRECTORY-006's GRANT_EXPIRY does; no sleeps.

K8, every refusal names the act that answers it and its leg asserts that act: StoreKeyMissing says supply the store key file at start, StoreKeyRetired says use the current key, every-account-rested says bring an account back, and so on through :109, :111, :113, :158, :198, :234, :268 and :303.

K9, every counted leg gets a runnable command and an exact expected result, for example cargo test -p lys-secrets --all-features --test store_leases sec3_store_ -- --include-ignored printing N passed, 0 failed, 0 ignored. R2's document checks (:76-86) either become heading or id searches with expected counts, or say plainly that the lead checks them by reading.

K10, "planted in the store" (:116 and the canary legs of R4 to R8) contradicts digest-only storage: the canary handle is issued through the broker and presented.

K11, a leg for R3's retry rule (:109): the same operation id returns the first outcome with the use count still 1, and the same operation id under a different handle or identity is refused.

K12, rollback. The sealed binding stops a swap between entries but not someone restoring an older ciphertext of the same entry: rollback joins the attack list (:85), and either a version or sequence is bound into the sealed prefix with a refusal leg at :111, or the contract records it out of scope.

K13, canary searches also look for lower- and upper-case hex and for standard and URL-safe base64 (:112, :114, :116 and the rest), so a hex-written key or a Basic auth header cannot pass.

K14, R2's handle clause (:78) sets at least 32 bytes from the OS secure random source, because an unsalted SHA-256 of a short handle can be brute-forced; the handle id is generated separately and never derived from the handle; one assertion checks that no audit line carries the handle's digest, which :82 forbids and nothing tested.

Three suggestions from the same review, not blockers, which the author takes or records as not taken with a reason: SEC3_STORE_KEY also searches the log directory; the contract covers audit-key rotation and what happens if the audit key is compromised; blocker check (a) checks each path separately.

The re-fire 18b96d68 was taken back before it published so these corrections ride with the RM-013 ruling in one run, at main 1756688. The tick still waits on Tom's word on ADR-019.

The lead's answers: SECRETS-003 keeps ADR-019 (proposed, amending ADR-001, waiting on Tom's word) and ADR-020 (decided); R5's OAuth refusals gain the same three presenter legs as R4, R6, R7 and R8; a stale presentation gets its own refusal leg on the injected clock in every row that carries a presenter check, so R4 to R8 assert 10, 9, 8, 10 and 8 refusals; and a sequence is bound into the sealed prefix, so an older ciphertext of an entry restored in place is refused by name.

items.title: LanternData carries lit_in, the light act records it, recall reports it and the fork reads the typed field
items.summary: A lantern records the session it was lit in. LanternData gains an optional lit_in; the light act writes it as the id of the session at whose head it appends the lantern and prints it in its report; recall rows carry it beside point, note and lit_by, null for a lantern lit before it; and HOME-006's fork reads it through a narrower typed view in place of the raw-data stopgap, with L2 in both fork fixtures lit by the light act and only the records the light act cannot produce written by hand. A lantern with no lit_in stays an older record resolved by its holders (ADR-017), and a present lit_in that is not a session id is refused lit_in_not_a_session by the fork and by recall, never read as any session (ADR-046).

provenance.quote: The lantern's typed data does not carry lit_in and the light act does not record it, so HOME-006's fork reads lit_in from the entry's raw data as a stopgap and the fixtures write L2 by hand. This card makes the typed field the shape. LanternData gains lit_in, the session that held the point when the lantern was lit; the light act records it at the head of the session holding the point; recall reports it beside point, note and lit_by. The fork in HOME-006 reads the typed field and its hand-written fixtures light L2 with the light act instead. A lantern record without lit_in, or with a lit_in that is not a session id, is refused by name as it is today, never read as any session. Ordered after HOME-006 lands. Acceptance: a lantern lit with the light act recalls with lit_in equal to the lighting session; the fork's fixtures contain no hand-written lantern entry; the two lit_in refusals keep their tests; the existing lantern and fork tests keep passing; ADR, checklist and user story rows renumbered past HOME-006's.
provenance.context: The Lys board card 0a59xZFp that HOME-006's third amendment names as the closer of the lit_in gap, surveyed on lys main 7b536253 with HOME-006 landed. Written again by the brief chain after run b9d7f174 wrote its brief under ids other open branches held. The lead's rulings settled that a lantern with no lit_in keeps the holder rule rather than being refused (correcting the request's 'as it is today'), that lit_in is optional and shows as null in recall for an earlier lantern, that the fork fixtures keep hand-written only the lanterns the light act cannot produce, that the two key-set pins and the light report's pin gain lit_in, that recall refuses a present lit_in that is not a session id as lit_in_not_a_session with the fork's four reason texts, and that every id is the next free past main and every open brief and draft head. The lead's answers to the survey settled that the tests whose fixtures change assert the id the light act returns in place of the literal L2, and that the fork reads a narrower typed view not requiring lit_at or note. HOME-014 carries those answers.

provenance.quote:
The brief for this card already stands in the cluster: docs/design/directory/briefs/DIRECTORY-002.json and DIRECTORY-002.md, "Install the standalone service dependencies on one PostgreSQL database", Row 02 of IDENTITY-001 revision 5, on main. This card rewrites it in place with the lead's rulings E1 to E11 below and nothing else, keeping its id, its path and its four requirements. Keep its four requirements exactly: R1 package Rauthy, SpiceDB and one PostgreSQL database and install them for development; R2 prepare, configure and check the deployment from the lys CLI; R3 theme both Rauthy clients with Aion's vocabulary and each product's own accent (ADR-010: every product shares one design and keeps its own accent); R4 state what SpiceDB enforces in step 1 and hold to it. Keep its boundaries and verification as written except where E1 to E11 say otherwise, and change nothing else that the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py, render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh) does not require. Facts the brief already settles, which the survey must not reopen: PostgreSQL may live on one of the network devices and the host is confirmed with the operator before anything is installed; the install runs on a node the operator names (ADR-005) with test identities only; the Rauthy installed is the maintained fork (ADR-009) at its pin from Row 01; one PostgreSQL holds both Rauthy and SpiceDB. Nothing here is a production node, no production key is generated and no receipt is emitted outside a test; those three acts are Tom's. If the survey finds a sentence of DIRECTORY-002 open or contradicted by the repository as it stands, quote that sentence as a question for the lead rather than rewriting the brief around it. This card supersedes the archived board 2 twin "Install the three services on one PostgreSQL", whose sign-off carries over.

This card is re-fired at main on 26 September after its first run, 7e9506d8, published a rewrite of DIRECTORY-002 at 3fe22ceb on a base 22 commits behind main. The lead ruled at 20:31 that the rewrite is not signed off and that every answer from that run's seven rounds is carried here as a settled ruling, so the author writes straight onto main with them in hand and reopens none of them.

E1 (round 1, answered by the lead, 26 September 16:02, as the published brief at 3fe22ceb records it). Unit tests sit in sibling *_tests.rs files under crates/lys/src/identity/, a wall revision under CN9; the themes are dark only, from the estate tokens as they stand, a Rauthy field taking a token only where the estate names the same role, with light mode, the error colour, the radius and the dark text_high, action and button text named as gaps for a design-system card; the platform and Cambium clients are the two managed clients beside the built-in rauthy client the pinned Rauthy's own migration inserts; the container-backed tests run in their own leg of .land/gates.sh and cargo test stays hermetic; the three blocked_by entries stand as written and each is discharged only by its blocker having landed, checked live when the build starts.

E2 (round 2 ruling, 18:31, coverage order). Accepted. The break is real: an acceptance line may not lean on a file only a later requirement owns. Fix it as the second correction says, by giving R1 and R3 the manifest themselves, and keep the requirement order R1 to R4 as it stands.

E3 (round 2 ruling, 18:31, the manifest). Accepted. Add modify: crates/lys/Cargo.toml to R1's files and to R3's files. R2's modification of the manifest stays as it is; three requirements may each add their own entries to one manifest in order, and none reads an entry a later one writes.

E4 (round 3, 19:07, dark field mapping). Map a Rauthy field only where an estate token names the same role, and record every other field as a gap, as the ruling on backgrounds says. So: text takes text, since Rauthy's text is the body text and the estate's text is its primary text; bg_high takes raised, the highest of the three backgrounds; text_high, action and btn_text are gaps, because the estate names no emphasised text tier, no accent and no text-on-accent. E5 (round 3, 19:07, the clients). Exactly two managed clients beside the built-in one. Write the acceptance as: after two configure runs against the same Rauthy, the platform client and the Cambium client each exist exactly once with the configured values, the built-in rauthy client is unchanged, and no other client exists.

E6 (round 4, 19:22, the theme decision and the ledger; its number amended by the lead's 20:31 ruling). E11 (Archie, 26 September 21:53, under the lead's 20:31 id rule and her 21:50 ruling that the adopt road built none of E1 to E10). This card's brief is not adopted. The author rewrites DIRECTORY-002 in place at docs/design/directory/briefs/DIRECTORY-002.json on main 1756688, keeping its id, its path and its four requirements, and changing only what E1 to E10 require. RM-011 in E7 and E8 is HOME-008's row, signed off on brief/home/5898fcb0, RM-012 is translate's on brief/home/f1228b7c and RM-013 is SECRETS-003's by the lead's 21:07 ruling, so the row E7 appends is RM-014, after RM-013, and wherever E7 and E8 say RM-011 the brief says RM-014. items.title: Translate a session imported from Claude Code into a Codex rollout with a loss account
items.summary: Stage 4b of the home: lys-home translate-codex renders a session imported from Claude Code as a Codex 0.156.0 rollout in the shape Codex writes for its own threads, carrying every text part, tool call and tool result whole, readable thinking as text and sidechains as marked text, with a JSON loss account beside it of what was kept, changed and lost by entry id and hash, a lys.translation side leaf on the session, and a resume on Codex 0.156.0 measured in a scratch Codex home. The Codex thread is a fork of the session, never the same session.

provenance.quote:
Translation is designed and not proved: the lantern work measured three session formats and left the converter out, so the first translation is one named pair, one session, and an account of what was kept, changed and lost, and nothing above it assumes it. The pair is Claude Code to Codex, the pair the lantern work measured: Codex's own importer of Claude Code files is the recorded baseline, a compaction and not a copy, dropping thinking, sidechains and meta records and clipping tool calls and results, and Tom ruled on 5 September 2026 that we improve on it and do not adopt it. This card renders a home session that was imported from Claude Code as a Codex rollout that Codex 0.156.0 on this Mac resumes, with a loss account beside it. A lys-home subcommand takes the home, the session, a target directory and the Codex version it renders for, walks the context path as the Claude Code render does, and writes a rollout file in the shape that version of Codex writes and reads for its own threads, measured from the files Codex writes here and never assumed from the June checkout; every text part is carried whole, every tool call and result is carried whole as Codex's own items for a call and its output and never as a truncated note, and readable thinking is carried as text while opaque blocks are dropped and named by hash in the loss account, as P3 rules for another provider. The rendered thread announces itself in band as a translated context with the source session id and the render's template hash, following the marker precedent, so the fork can never mistake itself for the original. The loss account is written beside the rollout as JSON and lists, by entry id and block hash, what was kept, what changed shape and how, and what was lost and why: sidechains, harness events, lanterns and other lys entries, and any block kind Codex has no item for. The report is JSON with the rollout path, entry and block counts, the loss counts and the account's path, never content. Acceptance is that a fixture session imported from a fixture Claude Code file renders to a rollout whose items match a recorded fixture rollout for Codex 0.156.0 apart from ids and timestamps; that the loss account names every dropped block by hash with a reason and every changed block with its before and after kinds; that a session with a thinking block from another provider renders it as text and the account says so; that a tool result longer than Codex's importer clips is carried whole; that rendering to an existing path is refused by path and writes nothing; that the rendered rollout is resumed by Codex 0.156.0 on this Mac and answers from its content, recorded in a proof document with hashes, counts and paths only; and that the Claude Code render of the same session is unchanged, checked by hash. Not in scope: Codex to Claude Code, which does not exist in any tree here; adopting or calling Codex's importer; Pi or any third harness; launching Codex through the launch template, which is that template's next version. Filed by Archie on Tom's roadmap stage 4b of 22 September 2026 at 14:45, his 5 September 2026 ruling on the Codex converter, the lantern design's session-formats measurement, and home DESIGN P1, P3 and P7 at lys main 0073b966, on 26 September 2026.

Corrections from Waffles' cross-review of the brief at db97e15 on 26 September 2026 at 19:24, carried into the words for the re-fire on lys main 1756688. C1: R5 counts as changed, naming the field in how, every part that lost or changed a field: a tool_use that loses its caller field, a one-item text array result written as a plain string, and an assistant turn whose model, usage and stop reason go nowhere; none of these is kept. C2: the session_meta line does not copy model_provider, source, thread_source or history_mode from the Codex fixture, values the Claude session never held; each is either named as a changed entry-level line with before none and after the key, or left out when Codex resumes without it. C3: every R2 refusal names the act that answers it, and the acceptance lines assert those words: UnmeasuredCodexVersion says render for 0.156.0 or card a measurement of the new version; BlockNotStored says re-import the source file; UnknownTimeZone and UnnamedTimeZone say set TZ to an IANA name; Exists says choose another --out. C4: R1's fixture recording and R10's resume spend Codex model requests, and the Codex account Chippy and Gypsy use has been at its usage limit since 26 September and resets on 30 September; the brief names the account it uses, checks at its start that the account can make requests, gives the refusal words and the act that answers them, and bounds R1's record-again loop with a stated count. C5: the thread id is record_uuid of the session head, so each head makes a new Codex thread and its turns never come home once Codex continues it; the brief states plainly that the Codex thread is a fork of the session and not the same session, and that the durable link back is the account and the side leaf, not the marker text, which a Codex compaction can erase. C6: every requirement names its command and its exact result, for example cargo test -p lys-home --test codex_translation with the test's name printing 1 passed and 0 failed, and a grep -c on PROOF-TRANSLATE.md for each field it must hold; this covers every R1 line, R4 to R8, and R10's proof checks. items.title: Hand an outgoing session's letter to a new successor home as inherited memory
items.summary: HOME-001 row R12, the handover, built as the lead's answers correct it. lys-home handover reads the outgoing session of a home without owning it and takes a letter: one or more assistant message entries standing next to each other on its path. It writes a new successor home holding one session: a lys.inherited entry with no rule naming the outgoing session and every letter id, then each letter entry copied whole with its thinking blocks and signatures, then a session_info named `inherited from` the outgoing session. It prints a JSON report naming the successor home, the session and its file, with inherited true read from the successor's first entry. A letter entry that is not an assistant message, a run that is not contiguous, an entry that carries provider authored, a letter with no thinking block, and a successor path that holds anything are each refused by name, and nothing is written. The canon loader newly refuses a canon example without a rule. PROOF-HANDOVER.md records the handover of a letter elicited for the purpose on the build machine, whether the installed Claude Code carries the inherited signed block into a resumed continuation's own file beside the version the row named, and the seeded and plain card counts as not run.

provenance.quote:
HOME-001 row R12 is the handover, and it is not built. An outgoing session writes one letter as its last turn, in its own words, saying what it knows, what it got wrong and why, how the people like things done and what it wishes it had known. A handover carries that letter into a new successor home as inherited memory, so the successor starts from what the outgoing session learned and never from a summary someone else wrote for it. Row R12 of HOME-001 on main at 7b53625 states the shape, and this card builds it as written.

The shape. A handover is one lys.inherited entry, followed by the letter's message entry copied whole, with its thinking blocks and their signatures and its text. The lys.inherited entry names the outgoing session as from_session, the letter's single entry id in from_entries, the letter's provider, api and model, the time it was written as curated_at, and the outgoing session as curated_by. It carries no rule. A letter is not a rule, and that absence is what tells a handover from a canon example. The command is lys-home handover with a home, a from session and a letter entry id. It copies that turn from the outgoing session into a new successor home as its first entries, the lys.inherited entry and then the message, and records in the successor's session_info that its first memory is inherited. The system never composes, edits or authors the letter or any thinking block, and it refuses by name a letter entry whose assistant message carries provider authored, writing nothing. When a successor is rendered for Claude Code, R4's rule applies. The inherited thinking renders whole only to the same provider, api and model, and otherwise renders as text with the opaque blocks dropped and named in the loss account.

The proof, in docs/design/home/PROOF-HANDOVER.md. It first measures whether the installed Claude Code replays a signed thinking block from a resumed file at all, on the version installed on the machine that measures, named in the proof. The row named 2.1.281, and the measurement is taken on whatever version the build machine holds, recorded beside the version the row named. The block is looked for in the continuation's next request as recorded by R10's proxy, or, until that proxy exists, by the harness's own file. It then runs one named card twice, seeded with a handover and plain, and records the counts of fix rounds and unverified claims for each, as counts only.

Acceptance, as R12 states it. Running lys-home handover on the walrus continuation's real letter turn produces a successor home whose first entry is lys.inherited naming that session and that entry, whose second entry is the copied message with a thinking block whose signature equals the source byte for byte, and whose session_info says inherited. Running it with a letter whose message carries provider authored exits non-zero naming the entry and writes nothing. PROOF-HANDOVER.md states the replay measurement and the two counts. Rendering the successor for a different model produces a loss account entry for the inherited thinking block and a text part in its place. Files are the ones R12 lists, handover.rs and PROOF-HANDOVER.md created, and entries.rs, cli.rs and RECORD.md changed. Keep to the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py, render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh). The brief id, roadmap row and any decision take the next free id after main's highest and every open brief/* and draft/* branch's, checked with git ls-remote immediately before writing. Not in scope are the little proxy R10, the canon R11 beyond the lys.inherited shape it already defines, and any change to how thinking blocks are signed or verified. If a sentence here is open or contradicted by the repository as it stands, the survey quotes it whole as a question for the lead. Filed by Archie, lead for the home line, on 27 September 2026 on lys main 7b53625.

Rulings of the lead, Archie, given on 27 September 2026 to the run 4c46aabc-6b23-48e7-9268-aea13019db4f in answer to its rounds. That run took every answer and then failed before writing, when the account pool refused every session. They are settled here, and the author reopens none of them.

The whole turn, never merged. The handover takes the letter as one or more entry ids, which must be a run of assistant message entries standing next to each other on the outgoing session's path, in path order. Each entry is copied whole, with its thinking blocks and signatures or its text as it stands, and from_entries lists every id in that order. Merging entries into one message would be composing the letter, which the words forbid, and copying one entry would lose either the thinking or the answer. Accepted, and closed by the same ruling. The acceptance measures the two-line numstat and the two added lines' contents.

items.title: Sign what a session was given at render, checked offline with lys verify
items.summary: The first of CONFORMANCE row 6.5's three signed statements: lys-home render-launch computes the SHA-256 of the lys.given entry's RFC 8785 data, reports it as given_sha256, and when given a key signs those bytes as a lys/attestation/v2 statement kept beside the lys.given entry and as the two files lys verify --attestation reads offline. A render with no key is unchanged and reports unsigned. Row 6.5 is partial until the start and role-move statements land with the START and ROLES cards.

provenance.quote:
Conformance row 6.5 says three things are signed statements checked with lys verify --attestation: the start of an agent, what the agent was given, and a move of its role. HOME-003 on main records what a session was given as a lys.given entry at render, listed and checked by hash, but unsigned. lys-core on main already signs and verifies attestations. Nothing yet turns the start, the given record or a role move into a signed statement.

This card makes each of the three a signed attestation in lys-core's existing format. The given record of HOME-003 is signed at render over the hash it already records. A start is signed when a launch is recorded, over the launch id, the agent's directory id and the given record's hash. A role move is signed when it is recorded, over the agent, the role, the version moved from and the version moved to. Each statement is appended where its record already lives, and lys verify --attestation checks it offline. The signing key is a test key in tests and in the proof, and production keys stay Tom's acts (row 6.6).

Acceptance is that lys verify --attestation accepts each of the three signed statements from a fixture; that altering one byte of each statement makes lys verify refuse it by name; that the given statement's signed hash equals the hash HOME-003 recorded for the same render; and that no statement carries a transcript line, a secret value or a credential, checked by a search of the fixture's statements for the fixture secret. The brief names row 6.5 as the row it passes. Where the start and the role move depend on records other briefs make (the START launch record and the ROLES version record), it signs the fields those briefs name and waits for them to land, each checked by a command a stranger can run.

Filed by Archie, lead for the identity and home lines, on 27 September 2026, against lys main 7b536253.

Rulings of the lead, Archie, given on 27 September 2026 to the run 5cceabf9-7264-45ec-99a5-ff2d547eabf5 in answer to its round 1. That run took every answer and then failed before writing, when the account pool refused every session. They are settled here, and the author reopens none of them.

The SHA-256 of the lys.given entry's canonical custom.data. The words' 'the hash it already records' is wrong about the tree, and the brief corrects the sentence. render_launch computes that hash, records it in its render record beside the template, session head and manifest hashes, and signs over it. The acceptance equality then compares the signed hash with that recorded value for the same render.

This card lands the given statement only. The start statement and the role-move statement are named under further units not written, each attached to the card that makes its record, the START card 98qkhhCb and the ROLES card Ink1H1Os, and each is written when that record lands. No signer is built over fields no brief names yet. The brief says plainly that row 6.5 is partial until those two units land.

The existing single message stands, because the non-oracle rule stands. 'By name' means the refusal names the statement file it was checking and exits non-zero with lys verify's one message, never which field or byte was altered. The acceptance corrects its sentence to say that.

The given statement is signed by the home's key, which in tests and the proof is a test key. The lys verify command without --cert proves only that some key signed, so the acceptance also checks the signer. After lys verify accepts the statement, a stated command compares the attestation's signer public key with the fixture's test public key and fails on a difference, and a statement signed by a second test key fails that line. Checking against a trusted certificate comes with row 6.1's --cert, and the brief names that.

It still records the unsigned lys.given entry, as today, so no existing run changes. With a signing key given it also writes the signed statement. The report says in words whether the render was signed or unsigned, so nobody takes an unsigned render for a signed one. Acceptance lines cover both, a render without a key reports unsigned and writes no statement, and one with the test key writes a statement lys verify accepts.

This card is the asking. CONFORMANCE.md row 6.5, marked test, is part of the conformance test Tom set as the definition of done, and Tom's word of 27 September at 12:49, relayed by Waffles, is to get it all done. The brief records that as the reason the home design's signing non-goal is lifted for the given statement, amends that non-goal line in docs/design/home/design.json to say so, and leaves anchoring and receipts into a lys log as non-goals still. HOME-003 line 218 is historical and stays.
provenance.context: The signed-statements card for CONFORMANCE row 6.5 on the Lys board, filed against lys main 7b536253 by the lead for the identity and home lines, with that lead's rulings on its first run carried into the card, and two further answers on this run: the given hash is recorded only in render-launch's report and in the signed statement, never in the kept template_render event; and lys verify's message stays unchanged, the stated acceptance command naming the file. HOME-016 carries those answers.

items.title: Run every test binary in the gate's test leg with --no-fail-fast
items.summary: The gate's test leg stops at the first failing test binary, so a red round hides every failure after the first. One commit changes it to `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast` in docs/design/project.json, the directory, home, secrets and lys-gate design.json gate arrays and .land/gates.sh, and, by the lead's rulings, in CLAUDE.md's 'Gates before any commit' block (so .land/gates.sh still matches it exactly) and CI's test step (which gains the one flag only; its missing --all-features is a finding left unchanged). Proved by a grep over the declared legs that prints 0, the green gate round's '$ command' line for the tests leg, one gate round over a local scratch branch with a planted failing test in crates/lys that never reaches origin, and a proof document that names that round's log by path, SHA-256 and counts.

provenance.quote:
The lys gate's test leg stops at the first failing test binary. Five files declare it as `cargo test --workspace --all-features`: docs/design/project.json (the project gate), docs/design/directory/design.json, docs/design/home/design.json and docs/design/secrets/design.json (the cluster gates), and .land/gates.sh (the landing hook). A run that fails in one crate reports nothing about the binaries and crates after it, so a gate can go red for one reason while hiding others.

This card changes that leg in all five files to `cargo test --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast`, in one commit. Every test binary then runs, every failure is reported in the one gate run, and the leg still exits non-zero if any test fails. Nothing else in the gate changes: the other legs, their order and their requirements stay exactly as they are. No timeout is raised and no test is split.

It is done when all five files declare the new command and scripts/design/gate.sh stays green. A check over docs/design/project.json, every docs/design/*/design.json and .land/gates.sh must show that no test leg there still runs `cargo test --workspace --all-features` without --no-fail-fast. The ledger that runs the gate recognises a battery by the text "cargo test" in a leg's command, so each changed leg must still be classed as a battery, shown in the gate log. One gate round over a scratch branch that adds a single failing test in one crate must show in its log that failure together with every other test binary measured; that branch is never landed. The briefs under docs/design/*/briefs and the release documents quote cargo commands as acceptance text or instructions, not as gate legs, and this card does not change them.

Keep to the method (scripts/design/validate.py, check-coverage.py and render-cluster.py, run by scripts/design/gate.sh), and render any cluster whose design.json changes. items.title: Move a home by a pushed git ref and resume it in a second home on the same machine
items.summary: The first block of the context roadmap's stage 3: a home becomes a git repository tracking exactly its session, index, head, block and template files; lys-home ship pushes it without force as the one ref refs/lys/home to a bare repository at a path on this machine, refusing by name an empty home, a stale or missing index or head, a held session, a foreign tracked file, a remote path that is not a bare repository, a diverged ref and any remote off this machine; lys-home fetch pulls the ref into an empty second home, verifies every index, head, block and template, hangs one arrival event with a fresh execution id beside each session's head, and commits the arrivals as one commit on the fetched commit; the fetched home is rendered through the Claude Code launch template and resumed on 2.1.283, measured as hashes, counts and paths.

provenance.quote:
A home is a directory of session files, their indexes and heads, and the blocks store, and today it lives on the machine that captured it and nowhere else. Roadmap stage 3 says a home moves by the same route as a build tree, a pushed ref that the target fetches, never a hand copy, and that the target gets a distinct execution id with its ancestry recorded. This card takes the first block of stage 3, the same-machine proof: a home shipped as a ref to a named remote and fetched into an isolated second home on this Mac, then rendered and resumed there through the Claude Code launch template. The home directory is a git repository whose tracked files are the session files, their index and head files and the blocks store; a lys-home subcommand commits the home's current state and pushes it as one ref to a remote named on the command line, refusing by name a home whose index is stale rather than shipping it, and reporting the commit and the ref it pushed. A second lys-home subcommand fetches that ref from the named remote into a new home directory that must not already hold a home, verifies every index against its file and every head against its index, and appends to each session a lys.harness_event recording the arrival: the source home's commit, the remote and ref it came from, and this home's own execution id, so the ancestry is on the record. Source files are never rewritten by either side, and no credential, token or secret value is ever tracked in the home. With the target home in place the launch template renders it and the printed launch line resumes it, which is the resume evidence stage 3 asks for, measured on this Mac on Claude Code 2.1.281 and written up as a proof document holding hashes, counts and paths only. Acceptance is that a fixture home with a synthetic session ships to a bare remote in a temporary directory and is fetched into a second directory whose session file, index and blocks hash-match the source; that the source home's files are byte-identical before and after; that the target session's last entry is an arrival event naming the source commit and a fresh execution id; that a fetch into a directory already holding a home is refused by name; that a home with a stale index is refused by name on ship and the report says so; that the launch template renders the target home and the launch line resumes it, recorded in the proof document; and that a search of the shipped ref for a fixture secret value finds nothing. Not in scope: the named second machine, which is stage 3's second block and waits on its two preconditions, read authority over the home from the directory step and encryption before bytes leave the machine from the secrets step, each a card on its own board, with this card's shipped ref as what that block fetches; harnesses other than Claude Code; encryption of the home; any transport other than a git ref to a named remote. Filed by Archie on Tom's roadmap stage 3 of 22 September 2026 and his 08:30 rule that a home moves as a pushed ref, on home DESIGN P1, P7 and P8 at lys main 0073b966, at 06:27 on 26 September 2026.

Rulings of the lead, Archie, given on 27 September 2026 to the run 65e82438-b7a0-4814-b3b0-b568b578d454 in answer to its rounds. That run took every answer and then failed before writing, when the Argus gate refused every tool call of its session. They are settled here, and the author reopens none of them.

Both, stated separately. The fetched commit's tree (before the arrival append) hash-matches the source for every session file, index, head and block. After the append, each target session file equals the source bytes plus exactly one appended line, the arrival event, and its index equals the source index plus that line's row. The acceptance asserts both, so nothing else differs.

Measure on 2.1.283, the version installed here, as PROOF-LAUNCH.md already did, and record that version in the proof. The words' 2.1.281 is superseded.

Yes. The templates/ directory is tracked and shipped with the sessions, index and head files and blocks, so every template_render event on the target names a template the target holds. The acceptance's hash-match covers templates/ too.

Initialise one. The first ship makes the home a git repository tracking exactly the named stores, and the report says it initialised. A home that is already a git repository with tracked files outside those stores is refused by name.

Refuse it. A session whose <id>.lock is held by a live owner is refused by name, naming the session, with the act that answers it: ship after that seat stops, or ship without that session. Ship never snapshots a session mid-append.

One per arriving session. Each arrival event carries a fresh execution id for that session's continuation on this machine, as the identity documents describe an execution per session or fork. No home-level id file. The ancestry a person reads is per session: the source commit, the remote and ref, and that session's new execution id.

Neither extreme. The ship command takes a remote that is a path on this machine, or an ssh remote whose host is one of the estate's own machines as named in this Mac's ssh configuration, as the second-machine proof needs. It refuses every other remote by name, remote_not_estate, whose words say that shipping beyond the estate waits for stage 3 encryption. That covers any https or git URL and any hosted service such as GitHub. Nothing leaves the estate unencrypted at rest. Each case gets an acceptance line: a local path ships, an estate ssh host ships, and an https remote is refused with those words, writing nothing. Answered by Archie, lead for the home line.

Remove it, but only if fetch created it, and only after the failure is recorded. The report is JSON naming the stale index or each block whose hash does not match its name, by hash and never by content, and records no arrival. A directory that existed before fetch is never removed, and fetch refuses a non-empty existing target at the start. The source stays where it was, so nothing is lost for inspection: fetching again reproduces the failure. An acceptance line asserts that the target is absent after a failed verification and that the report names the bad block's hash. Answered by Archie.

An explicit allow-list file in the home, and nothing else. The ship command accepts an ssh remote only when its host is named in <home>/estate-hosts, one ssh Host name per line, which a person writes. The ship command never infers the estate from ssh config, HostName addresses or a list of hosted services. A local path always ships. An ssh host not on the list, including github.com, is refused as remote_not_estate, with words naming the file to add the host to. A missing or empty list means no ssh remote ships. Acceptance lines: a listed host ships, github.com is refused with those words, and an ssh remote with no list is refused. Answered by Archie, lead for the home line.

Remove the files it wrote, and leave the directory empty as it was before. The fetch command records every path it creates, and on failure removes exactly those paths, deepest first, then checks that the directory is empty. It never touches a path it did not create. An acceptance line starts from an empty existing directory, fails verification, and asserts the directory still exists and is empty. Answered by Archie.

Rulings of the lead, Archie, given on 27 September 2026 to the run d5a29dc7-67e0-4ae4-ab7e-3ccf0ce201a1 in answer to its rounds. That run took every answer and then failed before writing, when its writer found no saved state for its session. They are settled here, they stand over any earlier ruling above that they contradict, and the author reopens none of them.

In this card ship takes a remote that is a path on this machine and nothing else. Stage 3's precondition stands as Tom wrote it, before any bytes leave the machine, and DESIGN.md:67 and the words' non-scope stay as written. The earlier rulings above on estate ssh hosts, the estate-hosts file and remote_not_estate are withdrawn. Any other remote, ssh to any host, https, or a hosted service, is refused by name as remote_not_local, whose words say that shipping off this machine waits for stage 3's encryption from the secrets step. No estate-hosts file is read or written.

The arrival event hangs as a side leaf beside the head, through append_beside, exactly as template_render hangs. The arrival is a fact about the record and not a turn, so the head file, the head hash and the next render's session_head on the target are the source's. Acceptance lines assert that after fetch the target's head file is byte-identical to the source's, and that a render of the target records the same session_head as a render of the source. This replaces the earlier ruling that each target session file equals the source plus one appended line.

When the remote path does not exist, ship initialises a bare repository there, pushes the ref, and the report names the path and says it created it. When the path exists and is a bare repository, ship pushes to it. When the path exists and is anything else, a non-bare repository, a file, or a directory holding other files, ship refuses by name, naming the path and what it found, and writes nothing. Acceptance lines cover the three cases.

There is no flag in this card to leave a session out. A session whose lock is held by a live owner is refused as session_held, naming the session and the act that answers it, which is to ship after that seat stops. The words 'or ship without that session' are dropped from the refusal. A later unit that adds such a flag settles what the commit holds for a session an earlier ship tracked, and the brief records that unit under further units not written.

The fetch command refuses a remote that is not a path on this machine as remote_not_local, with the same words ship uses, writing nothing, so the two commands read the same. One acceptance line gives fetch an https remote and asserts the refusal by name and that the target directory is untouched.

The brief that wrote an id first keeps it, and HOME-008 to HOME-012 are held on open branches, so this brief takes the next free home id past main and every open brief and draft branch, re-checked with git ls-remote and a fetch of every head immediately before writing, with the heads read recorded in the dev record. Every reference in the brief, the ledger and the rendered files follows the new number, the same rule the RM, ADR, C and S ids here already follow.

Rulings of the lead, Archie, given on 27 September 2026 to the run 0ea42811-aea6-40aa-8c70-67f6362f52a2 in answer to its rounds. That run took every answer and then failed before writing, when the account pool refused every session. They are settled here, and the author reopens none of them.

Only by lys-home writing none, as CN8 gives, and the brief says so plainly. Ship does not scan tracked files for secrets. Blocks hold imported tool results verbatim and a template's env and mcp slots are free strings, so a secret a tool printed or a person typed can be in the home, and no scan can promise to find every such value. That is why ship in this card takes only a path on this machine, and why shipping off the machine waits for stage 3's encryption. The brief corrects the words' sentence to say that no credential lys-home holds is ever written into the home, and it names the verbatim blocks and the free template slots as the reason ship stays local. The fixture acceptance stays as it is. Answered by Archie, lead for the home line.

Ship refuses by name and never overwrites. It pushes only a fast-forward. When the remote's ref holds a commit the new commit does not descend from, ship refuses as ref_diverged, naming the ref, the remote's commit and the new commit, and writes nothing to the remote. An acceptance line ships two unrelated homes to one remote path and asserts that the second is refused by name and that the remote's ref still names the first home's commit. Answered by Archie, lead for the home line.

items.summary: One audit receipt of IDENTITY-001's shared shape for every sign-in and every permission change: signed by the service that performed the operation and never by the party it is about, returned beside the signed event appended to the lys log in operation order, and checked offline by lys log verify receipt, which needs only the log and the service's public key and refuses a payload-commitment mismatch under the published CLI's one refusal class. provenance.quote:
Every sign-in and every permission change on the platform leaves an audit receipt, and this card writes the brief for that receipt and the code that emits and verifies it. The receipt's shape is the shared contract IDENTITY-001 already names: a version, a stable operation id, the actor, the affected identity, the operation, a commitment to the payload, and the log coordinate where the record sits; the brief carries that contract as written and adds nothing to it without a lead's ruling. The operations that must emit one are a person signing in through Rauthy (success and refusal), a provider being linked to a person, a grant being given or taken away, an agent being provisioned, and an identity moving between lifecycle states; each receipt is signed by the service that performed the operation, never by the party it is about, because a claim must not be settable by the party being judged. items.title: Sign each call, harness event and home-recorded open of a home into a lys log under the agent's identity
items.summary: lys-home's lys.call and lys.harness_event entries, and a lys.open entry for each sealed record opened through a new lys-home open, each append one leaf to a lys log the home keeps under its agent's identity: a typed payload of the identity event envelope carrying the session id, the entry id, the kind and the SHA-256 of the entry line, never content, signed with the agent identity's Ed25519 key through sign_attestation; a line a fork copies gets its own copy leaf naming the parent's leaf, or the checkpoint leaf and the line's position when the parent entry predates the checkpoint. lys-home log-enable --agent names the home's agent in log/agent and starts the log with a signed checkpoint covering what the home held before it, and is refused without the agent's key; a home never enabled appends as today. A failed append is refused naming the entry and holds the session pending at log/pending/<session id>.json until its leaf is written; an append to a logging home whose key is absent is refused before its line; lys-home verify checks a session against the log. Built after DIRECTORY-003 R2's envelope and F-BV2vqP's lys-log-store 0.3.0 land.

provenance.quote: lys-home records proxy calls as lys.call entries (ingest_call and ingest_outcome in crates/lys-home/src/record/call.rs) and harness events as lys.harness_event entries in the session JSONL. Its Cargo.toml depends on neither lys-core nor lys-log-store, so no entry is signed and none reaches a lys log. The repository has no server or runtime process: crates/lys is the verifier command line, and `lys log append` appends a leaf file without signing it. Opening a sealed record (`lys open`, seal::open_and_verify) leaves no record at all. The outcome: each lys.call entry, each lys.harness_event entry and each sealed-record open appends one leaf to a lys log under the identity. The leaf carries the session id, the entry id, the kind and the SHA-256 of the entry line, never content, and it is signed with the identity's Ed25519 key through sign_attestation, in the envelope the identity audit events use. A failed append is refused by name with the entry id, and the entry is never reported as recorded. Tests: two calls and one event give three leaves that verify under the identity's public key; one byte changed in an entry line makes verification refuse and name that entry; ingesting the same call_id again adds no leaf; a search of the log for a fixture message's text finds nothing. It builds after the identity event envelope (DIRECTORY-003 R2) and after the log grows past memory (F-BV2vqP) have landed. Not in scope: the door's proxy and the runtime, which live outside this repository, and anchoring, encryption at rest, and haematite as the store.
